title: Synthesis --- You Can Hear Which Past It Is

lessons.title: Practice — six singular patterns, no hidden vocabulary
lessons.gloss: a singular checkpoint for regular and strong completed-past patterns

segments.text: This checkpoint adds nothing. Retrieve only the three singular persons of each learned row. Every word in the short sentences is already known.

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: the complete frame for this chapter

segments.text: Regular rows:
yo: hablé, comí, viví.
tú: hablaste, comiste, viviste.
él / ella / usted: habló, comió, vivió.
Strong rows:
yo: tuve, hice, estuve.
tú: tuviste, hiciste, estuviste.
él / ella / usted: tuvo, hizo, estuvo.

The -er and -ir rows share -í, -iste, -ió. The three strong rows share -e, -iste, -o, but their stems must be learned: tuv-, hic-/hiz-, estuv-. Plural persons, more strong verbs, and new time or setting vocabulary remain outside this checkpoint.

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: let spelling show the stress

segments.text: Regular comí, comió, viví, vivió carry written accents for final stress.
Strong tuve, tuvo, hice, hizo, estuve, estuvo carry no written accents; stress remains in the strong stem.
Comiste and viviste need no accent because their ordinary stress is already next to last.

The regular -er/-ir endings continue Latin perfect material reshaped across Romance. Tuve and hice continue older strong-perfect histories, also reshaped rather than copied letter for letter. Estuve shows especially clear analogical remodeling beside the -uv- family of tuve.

segments.instruction: “Hice café. Viví en Madrid. Estuve bien.”
segments.source: [YOU SAY: “Hice café. Viví en Madrid. Estuve bien.”]

segments.prompt: Which pair carries written accents: comí/comió or tuve/tuvo?

feedback.correct: Right: comí and comió mark final stress; tuve and tuvo do not.
feedback.incorrect: The regular final-stressed pair carries the marks: comí and comió.

segments.prompt: Which learned form is especially described as analogically remodeled beside tuve: comí, hice, or estuve?

feedback.correct: Right: estuve was analogically remodeled beside the -uv- strong family.
feedback.incorrect: Look for the form sharing -uv- with tuve: estuve.

segments.text: Give the regular comer and vivir sets. (Comí, comiste, comió; viví, viviste, vivió.) Give the three strong sets. (Tuve, tuviste, tuvo; hice, hiciste, hizo; estuve, estuviste, estuvo.) Which rows share endings? (-er/-ir share one regular set; the strong rows share another.) The next chapter can add a new past contrast without borrowing any plural form here.

lessons.title: Synthesis — you can hear which past it is
lessons.gloss: synthesis — two pasts with two histories, and you can hear which is which

segments.text: Nothing new in this chapter. Say comí, then tuve.

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: the stress tells you everything

segments.text: Say those two again and listen to where your voice lifts.
comí — the stress lands on the ending. tuve — the stress lands on the stem.
That is not a detail. It is the whole difference between the two kinds of past in this chapter, and it is audible before you know anything else about the verb.
Endings stressed becomes the regular preterite. It needs a written accent, because Spanish marks a stressed final vowel: comí, viví.
Stem stressed becomes a strong preterite. It needs no accent at all: tuve, hice, estuve.
So the accent is not extra spelling to remember. It is the stress, written down. If a preterite has no accent, the stress moved back onto the stem, and you are looking at one of the strong ones.
The two kinds have two histories.
The regular preterite is Spanish doing what Spanish does: one set of endings, and — as in the present and the imperfect — -er and -ir agreeing with each other rather than going separate ways.

The strong preterites are older. They are Latin's own perfect, carried through with the stress where Latin had put it, on verbs used too heavily ever to be rebuilt. Which is the same reason the imperfect has only three irregulars: the words people say constantly are the ones that keep their odd shapes.

segments.instruction: comí, viví — and feel the lift on the last syllable
segments.source: [YOU SAY: *comí*, *viví* — and feel the lift on the last syllable]

segments.instruction: tuve, hice, estuve — and feel it move back
segments.source: [YOU SAY: *tuve*, *hice*, *estuve* — and feel it move back]

segments.text: Until you can place a preterite by ear before you place it by rule.

segments.prompt: A preterite with no written accent. Where is the stress, and which kind is it?
acceptedResponses: on the stem, a strong preterite

feedback.correct: Yes — no accent means the stress moved back onto the stem.
feedback.incorrect: On the stem, which makes it a strong preterite.

segments.prompt: Why does comi carry an accent when tuve does not?
acceptedResponses: the stress is on its final vowel
because the stress is on the ending

feedback.correct: Right — the accent is the stress, written down.
feedback.incorrect: Because comi is stressed on its final vowel and tuve is not.

segments.prompt: In the regular preterite, do -er and -ir take the same endings?

feedback.correct: Yes — as in the present and the imperfect.
feedback.incorrect: They do, exactly as in the present and the imperfect.

segments.text: Where does the stress fall in a strong preterite? (On the stem.) What does a missing accent tell you? (That it is one of the strong ones.) And why do the strong ones exist at all? (They are Latin's own perfect, kept intact on verbs used too much to be rebuilt.)
